lines.note: Taikwai and taikwaina describe something on a large or magnificent scale. The Portuguese examples continue on the next row.
Large expense and great works illustrate the meaning. Gaſto has long s followed by t, not the OCR's garlo; the repeated adjective is divided Tai- / quaina.
Taikwaina hito is a magnificent and generous person. The damaged beginning is quaina, completing Tai- above, not an independent cu una.

Taikwan denotes a high rank or office, paraphrased by ōkina kurai and located at the imperial court below. Reinspection after the supplied NINJAL cross-check reveals the worn bowl and stem of a after qu, rather than the draft's i in Taiquin.

runs.text: ou cargo em caſa do Dairi.

lines.note: The gloss includes an office in the Dairi household or court. Dairi occurs inside Portuguese prose and is flagged as a whole-word font term; its locally italic appearance is preserved.
Tairaka and tairakana mean flat or level. The faint i in the first form is restored; praina and chãa remain the printed Portuguese forms rather than modern replacements.
Tairakani is the adverb corresponding to the preceding adjective. The worn ai sequence is retained in the complete headword, correcting Tiracani.
Tairage gives the verb for making level. The example begins ji wo, the ground as object; the printed spacing A prainar is retained.
Ji wo tairaguru means levelling the ground. The Portuguese matches both making it flat and bringing it to an even level.
A metaphorical extension is laying waste or destroying. The joined label permet. and the single long s in Aſolar are preserved.
Tairan is great disorder or disturbance, with ōkina midare as its paraphrase. The Portuguese noun continues onto the next physical row.
The definition adds a military upheaval or revolt. Reuolta retains historical u for consonantal v.
Tairei concerns declining age and is equated with toshiyoru, growing old. The headword's capital is restored, but no new full stop is supplied where the impression gives no secure one.
Enuelhecer completes the infinitive phrase for growing old. The upright S. is the written-register label.
Tairi denotes a great victory or triumph. The entry's second sense, profit, is introduced after the following example.
Tairi wo uru means obtaining a great victory. The historical initial v of vru and the divided Portuguese victo- are preserved.

runs.text: ria. ¶ Item, Grande ganho, ou proueito.

lines.note: Ria completes victoria, without the draft's extra p. A second sense is great gain or profit.

runs.text: Polla mayor parte, ou pouco meis,

lines.note: Tairyaku means for the most part or approximately. The complete headword is restored from the worn type; meis is retained as the visible Portuguese form rather than automatically regularized to mais.
Or less completes the more-or-less expression. This short row is the continuation of Tairiacu.
Tairyakuna describes something proportionate or reasonable. The headword begins with T and ends in na, not the OCR's F and ra; arrezoa- continues below.
Do completes arrezoado. Mediocre here supplies the gloss of moderate or middling proportion; the printed historical wording is preserved.
Tairyū means delay or remaining in place, paraphrased by todokowori and todomaru. The final r of todomaru is restored, and the headword's long-u mark is a caron.

runs.text: Deterſe, ou não ir a diãte.

lines.note: Tairyū suru means stopping or not going forward. The pilcrow is restored, while joined Tairiǔſuru and separate a diãte retain the printed spacing.
Tairon is face-to-face debate or contention, explained by mukai ronzuru. The headword has o, not u; the Portuguese word continues below.
Da completes contenda. The dispute is face to face; the two occurrences of rosto are read with the visible t forms rather than the OCR's rosſo.
Taisai denotes great learning or wisdom, paraphrased by ōkina chie. The final ai is abraded but supported by the following adjectival form; Taiſu is rejected.
Taisaina describes a person of great knowledge and learning. Peßoa retains the printed ligature, and the adjective matches the preceding headword.
Taisan is a great mountain, matched by ōkina yama. The worn i is included within the single headword rather than preserving a spurious Ta ſan boundary.
This homograph concerns departing or dispersing. Shirizoki chiru supplies the Japanese paraphrase; its i is restored instead of the OCR's a.

runs.text: ſe dalgum lugar pera ſe ir.

lines.note: The person rises from or leaves a place in order to depart. ſe completes the verb divided at the preceding line end.

Taisanboku is classified by the dictionary as a kind of cherry-like tree. The visible a corrects Taiſunbocu; the historical description is retained without substituting a modern botanical classification.

runs.text: Hũa eſtrella que eſtà no ceo, a-

lines.note: Taisanbukun is introduced through a star in the heavens. The following relative clause describes the cultic identification given by the dictionary.

runs.text: qual cà na terra os gentios venerão por hum Ca-

lines.note: The relative clause says that non-Christian worshippers on earth venerate the star as a kami. The historically polemical label gentios is part of the source's wording, not a characterization adopted by the note.

runs.text: mi que antiguamẽte foi Gizǒ boſat. ¶

lines.note: Mi completes Cami. The source identifies this figure with Gizǒ boſat, Jizō Bodhisattva; the visible initial is G and the long-o mark is a caron, not OCR C and circumflex. The full words are flagged for optional font review.
The divided Japanese phrase names the Taisanbukun festival or rite. Hũa maneira begins describing a kind of ceremony; it is not the OCR's A ſũa maneira.

runs.text: monia, ou ſacrificio que fazem a eſte Cami, em

lines.note: Monia completes ceremonia. The rite is described as a ceremony or sacrifice to this kami; Cami is a whole Japanese word embedded in Portuguese prose.

runs.text: que lhe offerecẽ, & queimão muitas riquezas.

lines.note: The worshippers offer and burn many valuables. The nasal mark in offerecẽ is faint but visible; muitas corrects the OCR's maitas.

Taisō and Taisona concern something on a grand scale, here great expenditure or costly work. Catachi is read as one word from its surviving strokes, not the OCR's ca achi; the unmarked o in the alternative is retained.

runs.text: de gaſto, ou obra de muito gaſto.

lines.note: De completes Grande. The alternatives are great expense or a work requiring much expense, not a new entry.

runs.text: Hum liuro de ſete que ha que

lines.note: Taisō mondō is identified as one of seven books in a set. The first long-o mark is a circumflex and the final one a caron; the subject of the books follows below.
The seven books deal with warfare. This line completes the title's bibliographical description without adding a modern identification to the canonical text.
The adjective points back to Taiſo. The reference word is printed without a secure accent here and is not normalized from the accented entry; it is eligible for whole-word font review.

runs.text: Taitai. Maxi votorimo nai cotouo yǔ.

lines.note: Taitai expresses a state with neither superiority nor inferiority. The Japanese paraphrase explains equality, and the Portuguese noun is divided I- / gualdade.

runs.text: gualdade entre os que jogão, quando não

lines.note: The equality is between players. The Portuguese verb reads jogão, with a nasal ending, rather than the OCR's jogẽo.

The players neither win nor lose; the usage is labelled as occurring in Ximo. The repeated example's first fragment is severely abraded: visible Ti is retained, although Tai is expected before taide below.
The example continues with the copula gozaru, not gozartu. The Portuguese describes being tied or equal; iguaes ends on this row and does not require the OCR's spurious terminal division.

Taitaina ninjū, alternatively ikusa, introduces equal forces or numbers. Enlargement supports ninju, but no secure long-vowel mark survives above its final u. The Portuguese fragment is read Ge and continues with te in column 2, evidently intending gente; no nasal mark is supplied above the damaged e.

runs.text: te igual dambas as partes, ou igual guerra, ou

lines.note: The opening te follows column 1's printed Ge; the intended word is evidently gente, although its nasal letter or abbreviation is not secure at the column end. The definition describes equal forces on both sides, then an equal war or battle; the physical transition is retained.
This short indented row completes the preceding Portuguese alternative, batalha. It is body text rather than a new entry or page furniture.

runs.text: Polla mor parte. ¶ Item, o ſuſtancial dal-

lines.note: Taitei is explained first as 'for the most part' and then as the substance of something. The second sense is introduced by a printed paragraph sign; dal- continues below.
The row completes dalgũa couſa, with a nasal mark over u. The word division across the physical rows is preserved rather than joined.
The synonym tayuru explains cessation. The alias marker is lowercase i, not capital I; the Portuguese has the printed double-s form in Ceßar and introduces an example with Vt.
The Japanese example concerns something transmitted until now. The ending taitenxi- is divided before ta on the next physical row; tç and the double t in qitatta are retained.

runs.text: As couſas que tègora vinhão por tradição

lines.note: The initial ta completes the Japanese past-tense example. Its Portuguese translation refers to things previously handed down by tradition; the historical form tègora is retained.
The translation says that those traditions ceased or stopped circulating. The first vowel is e, not the OCR's o in coßarão, and the double-s type is retained.
Taiteqi denotes a great enemy. The Portuguese reads inimigo, correcting the OCR's ininigo; the worn d in Grande is still identifiable.

The Japanese paraphrase means a great road. Enlargement shows Grarde: the second r-like type is anomalous or has lost the right stroke of an n. This graphic reading is retained rather than silently regularized to Grande; the initial r after G is present.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Polla mòr parte, ou parte principal.

lines.note: A second sense gives the greater or principal part. The grave accent in mòr and the paragraph sign are visible; this remains a continuation of Taito.
This Taitō names China. The headword's open, v-shaped long-vowel sign is transcribed with a caron, distinct from the circumflex in Vôqina above.

runs.text: Eſtar igual ou ſer da meſma qualidade.

lines.note: A separate same-spelled headword means being equal or of the same quality. Qualidade is one word despite abrasion around its medial letters; the OCR's internal space is removed.
The example describes equally matched opponents. The Japanese remains roman, while the following Portuguese translation begins in italic on this row.
The opponents are compared with wrestlers. The a in lutão is abraded, but the nasal ending and surviving spacing support that reading; the scan's short physical row is retained.
Taitocu is glossed as great advantage or benefit. The medial t is weak but present; this is a new flush-left entry, not a continuation of the equal-opponents example.
Tai-u is paraphrased as great rain. The headword has a hyphen, not the OCR's point, and the Portuguese chuua contains two u-shaped letters; no modern chuva is substituted.
The Japanese rain example is followed by the idiom 'rain by the bucketful.' The visible separation after Tai-v is retained, as are xagicuuo, long s in nagaſu, and the nasal abbreviation in cãtaros.
Tai-un is explained as great clouds. The headword shows a gap without a secure hyphen here, unlike the hyphenated repetition in the following example; that distinction is retained.
The example says that great clouds cover all directions. A small hyphen is visible in Tai-vn, and the final long vowel of vouô has a circumflex; the Portuguese sentence continues below.

runs.text: eſtẽdem, & fazem ſombra por todas as partes.

lines.note: The clouds spread and cast shade everywhere. The nasal abbreviation in eſtẽdem is preserved, rather than expanded to estendem, and the entire row is Portuguese italic.
Taixa is explained by 'great shrine.' The Portuguese starts its temple-or-house paraphrase here; yaxiro is an ordinary Japanese synonym and not an embedded Portuguese font-toggle term.
The temple is described as a house of Camis. Camis occurs inside Portuguese prose and is retained in the surrounding italic type, with the plural s supplied by the printed text.
This separate Taixa means a great vehicle or cart. The repeated headword is not merged with the preceding shrine entry; the damaged medial letters of Grande remain recoverable.
Taixei denotes great force or momentum. The initial is a worn T rather than I, and a faint circumflex is visible in Vôqina; the final Portuguese alternative continues below.
This short body row completes the force-or-impetus definition. The printed impeto is not modernized by adding an accent.
Taixen is a large vessel, supported by the Japanese synonym fune. The Portuguese embarcação has some broken ink in the middle, but its full sequence and nasal ending are readable.
Taixeqi is a great stone. The Japanese ixi retains the Jesuit x spelling, while the Portuguese pedra is a single italic word despite wear around the e.
Taixet is glossed as love, followed by an example of burning with love. The headword's damaged capital has a surviving top stroke consistent with T, not the OCR's F.
The first example is translated as burning in love, then a new Japanese example begins. The object-marked Taixetuo and tçucuru are kept as printed rather than respelled.

runs.text: Amar ſũmamente, ou moſtrar grande amor,

lines.note: This translates the second example as loving exceedingly or showing great love. The nasal mark in ſũmamente is retained and is not an ordinary dot or modern accent.
The translation adds a term of affectionate reception, then offers another example and an alternative introduced by l,. The damaged sequence reads Taixetni, not the OCR's spaced Tai cetni.

Vomô completes the alternative expression for loving from the previous row. The medial m is broken in the impression, but its strokes and the final circumflex remain distinguishable; Amar is the italic gloss.
This Taixi denotes a king's son. Rey is the historical Portuguese spelling; the large apparent gap after R is not a word boundary.
The verb entry gives its inflected forms and the synonym Mucǒ, meaning to face. The Portuguese ends fronte, correcting the OCR's frome; the caron in Mucǒ is visible.

The example means speaking directly to someone. Abrasion affects the middle of Fitonitaixite; the surviving letters, the repeated taixite below, and the gloss support the adopted continuous form rather than the OCR's disconnected fragments.

Alguem completes the first translation, then a Japanese example containing Deus begins. The Portuguese-derived name is inside a Japanese construction here, not a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Por amor, ou por reſpeito de Deos. ¶

lines.note: The example is translated as for love or respect of God. The next Japanese example begins with the divided name Ie-; the printed hyphen stays on this physical row.

runs.text: ſu Christo varerni taixerarete. l, Tai-

lines.note: The divided name continues as Iesu Christo inside a Japanese example. The damaged pronoun-like form is retained as varerni, rather than normalized to vareni or varerani; the Portuguese below refers to us. Taixerarete is the adopted honorific form, but its first r has a weak shoulder. Christo retains the short s visible before t, unlike the italic Chriſto below.

This row completes the alternative taixi tamaite and its Portuguese translation concerning Christ's love for us. The Japanese is roman, and the translation is italic; no modern accent is added to nos.
A separate verb entry equates taixi with motçu, 'have.' The example begins with bugu, arms or equipment, and the printed row-end hyphen is preserved.
The opening uo supplies the object marker after Bugu-. The Portuguese specifies offensive weapons; Tendo and offenſiuas have worn letters but remain legible in context and image.
This is a cross-reference rather than another example sentence. Taixi, ſuru is the cited lexical label and is retained in roman after the italic Vide,.
The Japanese paraphrase places something above the throne or raised seat. The long vowel in Taixǒ bears a caron; aſ- continues as ſento on the next row.
This completes aſſento alto, the raised seat in the preceding gloss. The row is an indented Portuguese continuation, not part of the next military title.

The flush-left entry is Taixǒ, 'captain,' not the OCR's italic Aaixo. A parenthesis and displaced continuation de, ou officio. sit far right on this same physical row and complete the following entry's dignida-; they are kept spatially separate rather than reassigned to that row.

Taixocu concerns a high office or dignity. The Japanese reads Vôqini tçucaſadoru without the OCR's internal break in Voqi ni; the faint circumflex and worn medial letters are adopted from the surviving type. The final dignida- connects to the displaced de above.
The small o types have weak upper outlines. Ooo 2 is the adopted reading of the gathering signature; the worn last o was recognized as u in the draft.
